en: Annotated Record of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s Attainment of Enlightenment Composed by Wang Bo of Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Written by Dàochéng, Master Huìwù of Quàn-Táng Yuèlún Mountain, who was conferred the purple robe.
Regarding Śākyamuni: this is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Capable Benevolence" (Néngrén). This is the clan name of the Transformation Buddha within the Sahā world.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama* (Cháng Āhán Jīng), in the past there was a Cakravartin King of the Ikṣvāku clan. Following his instructions... [text continues]
Due to the slander of the consort, the four princes were banished to the north of the Snow Mountains, where they established their own city and dwelt there.

Through their virtue, they attracted the people, and within a few years, they had flourished into a powerful nation. The father-king, filled with regret and longing, dispatched an envoy to summon them back. The four sons declined the invitation and did not return.
The father-king then sighed three times and said, "My son is Śākya," and thus he gave his clan its name. Thus it was for the Tathāgata.
The term "Tathāgata" (多陀阿伽度) in Sanskrit is translated as "Rulai" (如來) in the Qin language; it is one of the ten titles [of a Buddha].
It signifies that [the Buddha] has come from the path of suchness to achieve perfect enlightenment. To achieve the Way is what is meant by the Dharma King inaugurating his mandate.
Now, the Way of all Buddhas is a realization that is not attained through acquisition; it is not an ordinary way. Furthermore, this refers to the achievement of enlightenment by Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

The time since [his arrival] has been exceedingly long; it is not merely in this present life that he manifests a body through his great vows of compassion to transform beings and benefit living things, for there is also a beginning and an end to this process. Therefore, it is called "attaining the Way" (siddhi).
*History of the Tang*. Wang Bo was a *boshi* (Court Scholar) during the reign of Emperor Gaozong. He was the third son of Wang Fu.
Together with his elder brothers Boju and Bomin, he shared a reputation for talent; they were then known as the "Three Pearl Trees of the Wang Family.

In his youth, Bo was ranked among the four most famous writers in the realm alongside Yang Jiong, Lu Zhaolin, and Luo Binwang, and were collectively termed the "Four Masters" (*sijie*). During the Qianfeng era, the Prince of Pei heard of his fame...

Due to his talent and reputation, he was summoned to serve in the imperial administration. At that time, the various princes were fond of cockfighting; Lu Zongbo playfully composed the "Proclamation for the Prince of Ying’s Cock.
Emperor Gaozong became enraged, saying, "This is the very beginning of inciting strife," and consequently demoted him to the post of Administrative Assistant in Guo Prefecture.
His "Record of Tengwang Pavilion," "Record of the Śākyamuni Portrait," and the "Stele of the Vimalakīrti Portrait" all became widely circulated throughout the world.
"Observe how Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested his traces.
"Observe how" serves as the opening of the discourse. "Śākyamuni Tathāgata" is explained in the preceding note. "Manifested his traces" means:
Master Yu said: "I have heard that Bodhi, as the ultimate state, is divinely subtle, tranquil, and pervasive; its perfect wisdom is a profound illumination.
Its Way transcends the boundaries of form and consciousness, and its principle exhausts the realm of birth and extinction. How could it truly be born from a royal official?"
How could it be that the Truth has declined in the forest of Gu? It is only because I pity the myriad beings who have long been in slumber;

they shall together return to Great Enlightenment. When conditions arise, there is transformation; when resonance reaches its peak, there must be a response. If there were a response without birth, who would awaken the world? Though transformed, it remains nameless.
For what purpose does he guide the world? It is for this reason that he is designated as Śākyamuni. He takes his lineage from the Kṣatriya caste;

he embodies the most honored among those within the realm and stands as the preeminent excellence among humans and devas. Thereafter, he casts off his sandals in the prince’s palace and attains true contemplation beneath the Bodhi tree.

Abandoning the golden wheel, he governs the great trichiliocosm; manifesting the jade-white ūrṇā-hair, he brings the entire Dharma-realm under his command. This is how he manifests his traces in the world.
The body of the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-kāya) is fundamentally without appearance or disappearance.

Since one intends to record the beginning and end of its transformative traces, one first discusses the dharma-body (dharmakāya). Now, as for the dharma-body, it is the very essence of the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya);
it is the pure dharma-realm. It has many provisional names, which will not be enumerated here in full. The Qin monk Zhao said:

The Tathāgata takes the Dharma-realm as his essence; his form is omnipresent, and his measure exceeds the boundaries of the compass and square. His Way transcends the realm of speech and deliberation.
He is凝然湛寂 (nirvāṇa-like, profoundly still), neither form nor appearance; neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going.
Therefore, it is said that he is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing.
"Manifesting birth through the power of great compassion and vows" clarifies that there is appearing and disappearing.
Regarding "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*): it is one of the four immeasurable minds of a Buddha and is the root of the Buddha-way.
Its function is to uproot suffering; because this function is realized in the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "great. As for "vows":
This refers to the Great Vows. "Power" refers to the Ten Powers. Of these ten *pāramitās*, any two may be cited.
Now, because the Buddhas possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they do not abide in *nirvāṇa*; because they possess great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), they do not abide in *saṃsāra*.

Because they possess great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), they enter into suffering with unremitting diligence. Emerging from the ultimate truth (*tattva*) into the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), they manifest bodies through skillful means (*upāya*). Thus it is said:
Manifesting birth,
he reached the Tuṣita Heaven— Sanskrit *Tuṣita*,
or in Chinese *Dǔshìduō*, meaning "Contentment"— which is the fourth heaven of the Desire Realm.
It is a heaven. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This heaven is the most supreme within the desire realm;
therefore, Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood all manifest birth in this heaven for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings."
For the sake of the Bodhisattva Rakṣaprabha—
Rakṣaprabha being the name [of Śākyamuni] during his stage on the path of causes (hetubhūmi)— he encountered the Buddha Kāśyapa when the human lifespan in this Bhadrakalpa was twenty thousand years;
this was the name he bore at the time he received his final prediction of future Buddhahood, as well as at the time of his birth.

Tuṣita is also designated by this name. As for the present-day Maitreya, he is a Bodhisattva. In the Sanskrit language, the term is fully *bodhisattva*, which translates here as "Awakened Being" (覺有情).
This title is established based on his practice; it is now abbreviated as "Bodhisattva."
He descended upon the kingdom of Kapilavastu—Sanskrit:
*Kapilavastu*; Chinese: "City of Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode Cheng*)—which is Central India.
He was named Sarvārthasiddha ("Accomplisher of All Aims").
In Sanskrit it is called Sarvārthasiddha; in the language of China, it means "Accomplishment of All Aims.
This was the Buddha Śākyamuni’s original childhood name. It is sometimes abbreviated or corrupted as Siddha.

The *Śūramgama-sūtra* (Ruiying jing) states that when the Bodhisattva was born in the royal palace, five hundred boys were born on the same day among the Śākya clan within the kingdom, and five offspring were born to each elephant and horse in the stables.

Regarding "Hundred Colts": five hundred hidden treasures appeared within the ocean from within the palace. Five hundred merchants gathered these jewels and returned, each offering rare and precious items.
When the father-king beheld this auspicious event, he established this name for him. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
There are five causes for establishing a name: namely, based on birth, based on characteristics, based on a metaphor, based on contempt, and based on veneration.
The establishment of the Prince’s name was based on characteristics; that is to say, because at the time of his birth there were many auspicious signs.
The Devaputra Kanaṅkama selected his family.
The *Sūtra on the Original Acts* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states: "Vimalaprabha said to the Devaputra Kanaṅkama:

'In the past, the family into which a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood (*caramabhavika-bodhisattva*) takes rebirth must possess sixty kinds of merit and have three generations of purity. You shall descend to Jambudvīpa for this purpose.'"
I observed that in the city of Kapilavastu there was a king named Śuddhodana and a queen named Māyā;
they were pure and endowed with all virtues among all the worlds and possessed great renown. "It is fitting for me to be born into that family," said Vimalaprabha.
"Excellent! I shall certainly be born there," he replied.
King Śuddhodana was his father.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Śuddhodana, which here means "Pure Rice. The *Sūtra on the Original Acts* states that this is because his wealth and virtue were perfectly complete.
The jade elephant rides the sun.
Now, from the time Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested his birth in this land until its conclusion, there are eight phases: first, the phase of descending from Tuṣita;
second, the phase of being born in the Lumbinī Garden; third, the phase of touring the four gates; fourth, the phase of leaping over the city walls.

The appearance of renouncing the household life; fifth, the appearance of demonstrating the practice of the Way on Snowy Mountain; sixth, the appearance of descending from the Bodhi tree to subdue Māra and attain enlightenment;
seventh, the appearance of turning the Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park; eighth, the appearance of entering Parinirvāṇa beneath the Śāla grove—this is the first appearance.
The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) states: "The Bodhisattva shall proceed in the form of a white elephant to enter the womb. For what reason?"
Regarding the three animals crossing the river:
because the elephant reached the very bottom, he manifested his descent into the womb of Mahāmāyā.
*Mahāmāyā* in Sanskrit means "Great Illusion" (*Dàshù*) in Chinese; she was the Mother of the Buddha. This occurred in the city of Devadṛśa.
She was the eighth daughter of the elder Sujāta. An interpreter of signs prophesied, "This girl shall give birth to a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
When King Śuddhodana heard this, he took her as his queen. The *Sūtra of Past Deeds* (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) states:
"Queen Māyā dreamed that a white elephant entered her right side like the sun; she reported this in full to the king, who summoned the interpreters of signs to question them. They said: 'A girl...'"
"This person will surely be reborn as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin). Let us examine this briefly.

Does not the Sūtra state that for ninety-one kalpas a Bodhisattva does not fall into the evil realms? How, then, could he have a body in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a white elephant in his final birth?
However, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that this is not a literal fact; rather, it is because in that country, elephants are honored and highly esteemed, and thus [the Bodhisattva appeared] as one.
This dream is of great auspiciousness. It was manifested as such in order to prompt the interpreter to speak of it. A question is asked:
"Does a Bodhisattva in his final birth truly undergo conception? The answer is given in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"In order to bring to fulfillment those sentient beings of small minds and inferior understanding, [the Buddha] does not wish for them to think that these [Bodhisattvas] are spontaneously born through transformation, [but rather to show] their merit and wisdom."

This is not attained through cultivation; therefore, he manifests entering the womb. Furthermore, it is said that while the Bodhisattva is in the mother’s womb, his chamber and precious palace are exactly like a celestial palace.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he causes the mother no suffering or affliction.
Three times each day, the Buddhas of the ten directions enter to comfort him and preach the Dharma-gate of taking birth. Those who practice together throughout the ten directions likewise do so.
Bodhisattvas and all devas and humans all entered to inquire after his health and listen to the Dharma; by this clear evidence, it is known that this is not a reality.
[He] acts as a king with a golden wheel.

There are four types of wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*): first, the iron-wheel-turning monarch, who rules over one world-system; second, the copper-wheel-turning monarch, who rules over two world-systems;
third, the silver-wheel-turning monarch, who rules over three world-systems; and fourth, the gold-wheel-turning monarch, who governs all four world-systems.
He possesses seven treasures and a thousand sons. As for the seven treasures: first, the golden wheel; second, the jade woman; third, the horse; fourth, the elephant; fifth, the [jewel] master...

The treasure of the earth deity; sixth, the minister in charge of the military; and seventh, the wish-fulfilling jewel. On the day the noble king ascends the throne, these seven objects all arrive spontaneously from the sky.
By means of this, he traverses the four continents through the air. In all lands, upon seeing the golden wheel fly there, they all submit of their own accord.
The *Bonnōgyō* (Sūtra of Past Deeds) states: "Once the prince was born, those skilled in physiognomy declared that he was endowed with..."
The thirty-two marks are clearly manifest; he will surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
He was first born beneath the Ashoka tree.
This is the second sign of his descent into birth in the Lumbinī Garden. The *Ruiying Jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) states: "Lady Māyā..."

As the months of her pregnancy drew to a close, she desired to stroll in this garden. Upon arriving, she immediately raised her right hand to grasp a branch of an *aśoka* tree and gave birth to the Prince from her right side.
The Lord of Devas, wrapping his hands in celestial, exquisite garments, received him;
celestial beings held a golden-handled parasol, while devas, nāgas, and spirits scattered fragrant flowers and played music. Throughout the ten directions, the great earth...
There were six kinds of earthquakes and thirty-two kinds of auspicious omens; as the text is voluminous, these are not recorded here.
According to the *Jin gu lun heng* (Discourse on Weighing the Present and Past) and the *Zhou shu yi ji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou):

in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Ji Zhou dynasty, the year of Jia-yin, on the eighth day of the fourth month, rivers, streams, springs, and wells overflowed, mountains and valleys shook, the palace halls trembled, and the regular stars did not appear.
A light of five colors pierced the Dàwēi Palace. The King questioned his ministers, and the Grand Astrologer Sūyóu reported, "In the west, a sage has been born;
a thousand years hence, his teachings will arrive here. The King ordered that a stone be engraved and buried at the southern suburban altar to mark this event.
The eighty minor marks of excellence are like fragrant blossoms.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The eighty minor marks reside among the [major] marks; following the major marks, they adorn the Buddha’s body.
Regarding the term "fragrant blossoms" (*fenhua*), it corresponds to the Sanskrit *puṇḍarīka*, which means "white lotus. Nirvāṇa... [text continues].
The *Pán jīng* (Brahmajāla Sūtra) states: "The body of the Tathāgata is not defiled by the womb; it is like the *puṇḍarīka* flower, for its original nature is pure.
The thirty-two marks of a Great Being are as bright as the full moon."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "He manifested the thirty-two marks to adorn himself, like the full moon on the fifteenth night;
he then walked seven paces in each of the four directions."

The *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* (Ruiying jing) states: "At the time of the Bodhisattva’s initial birth, without anyone to support him, he walked seven paces in each of the four directions, with lotus flowers naturally appearing to receive his feet.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "He manifests in the world as being most peerless.
The *Vajrasena-avadāna* states: "The Tathāgata’s demonstrations of conduct are of three kinds: first, exercising supernormal powers to transcend..."
First, he travels through space. Second, natural lotus flowers receive his feet. Third, when walking, the soles of his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground;
the marks of the thousand-spoked wheels clearly imprint upon the earth.
Nine dragons together bathe his single body with water.

The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) states: "When the Bodhisattva was born, nine dragons descended from the sky, raining down a fine mist that was neither cold nor hot, bathing the Bodhisattva’s body."
The udumbara flower appears;
it is only when a Golden Wheel-Turning King is born that this flower manifests.

Because it is renowned in the world as difficult to see, it is used as a metaphor for the difficulty of encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world. Thus, the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (The Collection of Original Deeds) states: "Asita..."
The Seer said to the Great King: "Just as the udumbara flower appears only once in immeasurable, boundless billions of hundreds of thousands of years, so too is the Buddha.
The *Āgama* Sūtra says: 'One should regard the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world as being like the udumbara flower.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: 'The Buddha is like the udumbara flower; his encounter with birth is rare.'"
He let out a lion’s roar.
The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* states that at the time of the Prince’s birth, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, uttering this great lion’s roar:
“In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the honored one. Now, among the various beasts of the world, the lion is—
It is long. There are four things regarding its single roar: first, when the hundred beasts hear it, their brains split;

second, the fragrant elephants are subdued; third, the flying birds fall; and fourth, the aquatic creatures hide away. Now, the Buddha’s voice is used as a metaphor here specifically to signify fearlessness.
It likewise possesses four aspects: first, when the Buddha’s voice preaches the Dharma, the hundred dharmas are simultaneously shattered; second, the heavenly Māras are subdued...

First, the three external paths and false views are subdued; second, one falls away from them; third, all afflictions are subdued and severed; fourth, the Dharma and its metaphors are equalized—such is the case here.
It is said that once the stage of the womb is exhausted, one early on realizes the eternal body.
The "eternal body" refers to the Dharma-body of the pure Dharma-realm. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Since the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed. If this is so, then his stage of gestation has already ended and he no longer undergoes future existence; how then can he be born now?
From the time he attained liberation until the present, he has manifested his traces of transformation.
The mind of all Buddhas is precisely this great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, great compassion is likewise inexhaustible;
it is for this reason that he appears in the world to deliver sentient beings. Question: Since the Buddha has already attained the Way...
[Question: For a vast duration of time, you possess great sovereign power; why do you not simply manifest transformation and become a Buddha immediately?
Why must you enter a womb and be born from the side? [Answer: The *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* states:

"If a Bodhisattva wished to bypass birth from a womb and attain Buddhahood in a single instant, those sentient beings of small minds and inferior understanding might suspect this is a mere magical transformation and refuse to accept the teaching. If [he were so born]..."
If he were poor and lowly, it would be easy for him to leave the household life; people would say it was merely to avoid hunger and cold.
Therefore, he manifested entry into the womb and birth from the side into a royal family, following various worldly customs before finally renouncing the world.
Thereupon, he returned to his swaddling clothes and cradle to appear like an infant.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; it is not composed of blood, flesh, sinews, or bones.
It is only to accord with the ways of worldly sentient beings that he manifests as an infant. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) says: "That which is before the chest is called..."
He was wrapped in swaddling clothes; because his mother had previously nourished him with milk, he is called an "infant" (*ārbhaka*).
This was for the purpose of divination and physiognomy.
Regarding the sage Asita—*Asita* in Sanskrit, which in the language of China means "Incomparable"—he was a long-lived immortal (*ṛṣi*) from the Western Regions who possessed human lineage.
As a mirror for this, the *Sūtra of Fundamental Practices* (*Benxing jing*) states: King Śuddhodana summoned the seer Asita to examine the Crown Prince.

The seer wept and choked with emotion. When the king asked him the reason, the seer replied: "The Crown Prince possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all clearly manifest and distinct.
He is not one to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; he will certainly leave the household life and attain Buddhahood. Thus it was prophesied.
The Great Dharma-Wheel brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings. Now, lamenting my own advanced age, I grieve that I shall not witness the transformation through the Dharma;
having lost this great benefit, I am thus filled with sorrow and regret.
Regarding the account of his visit to the shrine, it is recorded that he was moved from his seat at the temple of Maheśvara.

The *Sūtra on Auspicious Responses* states: When King Śuddhodana prepared his carriage and took the Prince in his arms to pay homage to the temple of the deity Maheśvara, all the divine images rose up and prostrated themselves at the Prince’s feet. The King, filled with wonder and admiration, exclaimed: "My son..."
Among the celestial deities, he is most honored and supreme; thus, it is appropriate to style him "God among Gods" (Devātideva). This is the Buddha’s second minor title (*kṣudranāma*).
Alternatively, he may be a youth;
as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "He currently dwells on the stage of a youth, desiring to manifest mastery over all worldly affairs."
Because of karma, some study as śrāvakas.

In India, there are five sciences (*vidyāsthāna*) in the great treatises: first, grammar (*śabdavidyā*); second, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*); third, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*); fourth...

Logic (hetuvidyā), fifth, inner knowledge (adhyātmavidyā). Regarding the treatises on grammar (śabdavidyā), which explain etymology and glosses, only those who are exceptionally intelligent in India are taught them.
The Crown Prince studied all five branches of knowledge thoroughly; by mentioning one of these, the other four are implied.
This was for the purpose of military training; the arrow towers and arrow wells still remain.
The Prince’s teacher was Candraprabha (translated as "Endurance Heaven"), who taught him martial arts. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
When the Prince was fifteen years old, he competed in archery with the Śākya clansmen. With a single arrow, he pierced through seven golden drums, and with another arrow—
A single iron boar pierced through; the arrow emerged, struck the ground, and entered the earth. From the depths of the dark spring, water gushed forth.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, took the arrow and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he erected a stūpa to enshrine and venerate it. This was the first of the four stūpas on this celestial realm.
The place where the spring gushed forth is called Arrow Well by the people. [Recorded by] the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty during his journey to the Western Regions.
The record states: "The Arrow Well is located thirty *li* southeast of the city of Kapilavastu. Its water is as sweet as sweet wine;
those who drink it when ill are immediately cured. The people benefit from it even today."
It was for the purpose of competing in strength; the elephant tracks and the elephant pit still remain.
The Sūtra says: After the Prince, along with his younger brother Nanda and Devadatta, had gone out of the garden to compete in strength, Devadatta went on ahead.
He saw a large elephant blocking the gate; he struck it with his hand and killed it. Next, Nanda came out and saw the elephant; he reached out his hand and dragged it to the side of the road.
Afterward, the Prince came out and saw it; lifting it up with his left hand and supporting it with his right, he threw it over the city wall.
The elephant fell outside the city, causing the ground to sink; therefore, it was called the "Elephant Pit."
They experience sensual pleasures for ten years.
Regarding these five sense objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—there is no one born in the desire realm who does not crave them as pleasure;
therefore, they are called "sensual pleasures. The *Sūtra on Past Deeds* states: "While the Prince was in the palace, he was fully provided with the five desires and enjoyed himself."
For ten years he had not gone outside; thus it is said that he enjoyed bliss for ten years.
Now he goes forth on a tour of observation at the four gates.
This third phase of the tour of the four gates serves as the foundation for his renunciation.
He delighted in the body of a śramaṇa and felt weary of old age, sickness, and death.
"Śramaṇa" is a general designation for those who have left the household life as disciples. The *Sūtra on the Original Deeds* (*Prātimokṣasūtra*) states:

"While in the palace, the Prince’s pleasure reached its peak, yet he longed to roam the gardens. The King issued an edict to strictly purify the streets and adorn the parks and pavilions, and selected a wise minister."

He served as an attendant, prepared to provide counsel whenever requested. When they first emerged through the eastern gate, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven transformed himself into an old man, frail and leaning on a staff.
Upon seeing him, the Prince asked his attendants, "Who is this person? They replied, "This is an old man. He asked, "What defines one as an 'old man'?
They answered, "In the past, he was once young and vigorous; however, as cold and heat have alternated and passed, his blood and vital energy have declined."
Change. There is no one born into this world who can escape old age. Next, he went out through the southern gate. A celestial being manifested as a sick man.
The Prince asked, and the attendant replied, "This is a sick man. It is because his desires were not moderated and his diet was excessive.
The four great elements become unbalanced and transform into illness; tormented by manifold pains, there is no certainty as to life or death.
No one born into this world can escape it. Next, he went out through the western gate, where a celestial being manifested as a dead man. The Prince asked, and the attendant replied:
"This is a dead man. His lifespan has come to an end; his vital spirit has departed; the four great elements have separated;
and his six sense faculties are devoid of sensation. Though his parents, wife, and children cherish him with deep affection, none can retain him.

Among the people of this world, whether noble or humble, wise or foolish, none may escape death. Because of this, the Prince’s mind became disenchanted; he turned his carriage around and returned to the palace.

Someone asked: "The Sūtra says that the King issued an edict to strictly purify the streets and thoroughfares, so that not even a single fragment of tile, rubble, grass, or chaff was permitted to remain."
"How could there be anyone who is ill or dying dare to stand before the Imperial Carriage? He replied:
"The *Bodhisattvacaryā-nidāna-sūtra* states that the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven manifested through the power of conditions; only the Prince and his attendants saw them.
Even the fact that the attendants responded was brought about by the power of the devas. He asked: "Who were these devas, and why did they compel this matter?"
The answer is: they were all spiritual friends and kalyāṇamitras with whom the Bodhisattva had practiced together in previous lives.

Because they were sustained by their sincere vows, they constantly followed at his side and manifested various transformations, so that while the Prince was amidst pleasure, he would give rise to a sense of weary detachment and never forget his renunciation.
The Crown Prince next emerged through the northern gate. A celestial being manifested as a śramaṇa, holding a *khakkhara* staff and a begging bowl, walking slowly before the carriage.
The Crown Prince asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a śramaṇa, a disciple of the Buddha. The Prince asked, "What is the meaning of 'śramaṇa'?
He answered, "The three realms are tumultuous and the six destinies are obscured. One who realizes the mind and attains the fundamental source [is a śramaṇa]."
"Therefore, he is called a śramaṇa. Having finished speaking, he soared into the air and departed. The Prince gazed up at him with joy and said, "Truly, this is what brings fulfillment;
I shall practice and study accordingly. Thereupon, he returned to the palace.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Kṣāntivādin startled the celestial maidens by manifesting their ugly forms.
Consequently, as the Prince traveled through the four gates observing various signs, his feelings of both joy and revulsion intensified day by day.

With his head touching the ground, the five limbs fully extended, this is the supreme form of prostration within the Buddha-dharma; it is the ultimate expression of reverence.
This constitutes one of the five qualities of the requester. Because it possesses both self-benefit and benefit for others, whenever the Buddhas [act]...

All that has been spoken is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma. That Brahma Kings and Śakra, Lord of Devas, all observe and request [the teaching] refers to the meaning of skillful means (upāya) in speaking according to what is appropriate.
The Tathāgata reflects upon the universal principles of the Sugatas and accords with the excellent maxims of the ancient Buddhas, responding to the base desires of sentient beings.
"Tathāgata" refers to Śākyamuni; "Sugata" refers to the Buddhas of the past. This means that he has attained equal and perfect enlightenment.

Having already emerged from the long night of birth and death, and having perfected the merits of the two benefits through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one has successfully accomplished what was to be done;
thus, one is called "Well-Gone" (*sugata*). The universal regulations and sublime counsels are all the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
"Base desires" refers to the mind that delights in the Lesser Vehicle. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "I recall the past Buddhas and the power of their skillful means in their practice. I...
"The path now attained should also be explained as the Three Vehicles.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared and simultaneously uttered words of praise.
When the Tathāgata contemplated these skillful means, all the Buddhas of the ten directions manifested before him and praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
Śākyamuni, the foremost of teachers, employs skillful means to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
He divides the single Vehicle of Dharma to collectively transcend the realm of afflictions.
This is the opening of the gateway of skillful means. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Dharma of the One Vehicle is taught as three according to what is appropriate.
Within the realm of birth-and-death and afflictions, it is called the domain of worldly toil (*rajas*)."
From this, he rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and proceeded to the Deer Park.
This is the seventh [scene], the manifestation of turning the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park. Regarding "the Bodhi tree": it is the Bodhi tree at the place where he attained Buddhahood.
Having received the exhortation and being about to turn the Wheel of Dharma, he departed from beneath that tree; hence it is said "he rose. The deer...
The "Garden" (ārāma) is the very place where the Wheel of Dharma was first turned. The *Xiyu ji* states that it is located in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Long ago, when Śākyamuni Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in his previous lives, he manifested as a king of deer named Ruru.
Devadatta was known as the King of Evil Deer; he and five hundred followers each resided together in this forest.
At that time, there was a king named Brahmadatta who was hunting in this forest. Both deer kings and their retinues were caught within the encircling net.
Then, the King of Good Deer went before the king and addressed him, saying: "Great King, you have been hunting, setting fires across the plains."
"Following this, one thousand of my followers shall die today. However, since deer are many when dead, their meat will soon rot and stink.
I pray that Your Majesty will show mercy and grant permission for one deer to be provided daily for the royal kitchen. Thus, Your Majesty may have a meal of fresh meat."
"My followers merely seek to prolong their lives from day to day. The king approved of his words and granted his request. Within the two herds, one deer was designated for the solar disc each day;
he never dared to miss his turn. One day, it fell to the turn of a doe in the herd of ill-fated deer.
Because the doe was pregnant, she appealed to the king to extend the period until a later time. When her plea was not granted, she threw herself before the King of Good Deer. The king said, "Alas!"
"O compassionate mother! Your kindness extends even to that which has not yet taken form. You should set your mind at ease; I shall take your place.
At that time, the noble Deer King went of his own accord to the royal kitchen. The chief cook reported this, and the King asked for the reason. He replied: "Today it is the turn of a pregnant doe.
I beg that her turn be postponed; there is no one else suitable to take her place. Yet who among us does not cherish even a single day’s life?"

"I cannot bear this now, and I also fear that the offerings will be lost; therefore, I have come to the kitchen myself. I pray that Your Majesty will grant me leave. The King sighed and said, "Excellent!
You possess such a heart, whereas I am but a beastly one. I shall renounce the taste of meat and no longer provide daily offerings."

He then dedicated this grove as a deer park for their sustenance. The Buddha, observing that this site possessed past karmic connections, first preached the Dharma there to repay the debt of gratitude owed to the land.

During the three-month period, he tamed the faculties of the five companions; Kātyāyana attained liberation, marking the beginning of the Compassionate Honored One’s teachings and the first instance of awakening.
Regarding the name:

"The Three Months of Training the Faculties" refers to waiting for the proper time. The Buddha observed that the faculties and conditions of the five men were only just ripening, so he went to convert and deliver them.
Yet they still did not believe or accept [the teaching]. The Buddha manifested various supernatural transformations to train and discipline them; this took approximately three months. Then...
He turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths in its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Among the five men, Kauṇḍinya was the first to attain realization and obtain the pure Dharma-eye, immediately realizing Arhatship. The Buddha named him Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
In Sanskrit, *ājñā* means "understanding" (*huá yán*); thus, he was given this name because he was the first to understand.
The other four attained the Way one after another. As for Kauṇḍinya—also called Cunda—this means "Fire-Vessel.
It is likely that his ancestors took this as their surname because they served the sacrificial fire. That he was the first to receive ordination was due to past causes.
According to the *Caiguo jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect), when Śākyamuni was practicing the path as the Seer Kṣāntivādin in a certain mountain, at that time...
Kauṇḍinya was once a king named Kali, whose nature was violent and evil. One day, having taken his court ladies into the mountains, he grew weary from hunting and fell into a doze.
At that time, his attendants entered the forest to gather flowers; as they walked, they came before the hermitage of a rishi, who was preaching the Dharma to them.
After a long while, the king awoke and, not seeing his women, took up his sword and went searching for them. He saw them there...
In front of the Immortal’s Hermitage, the King asked in anger, "Who are you? He replied, "I am the Immortal of Endurance.

The King asked again, "Have you attained the meditative concentrations of the higher stages? He replied, "Not yet. The King said, "Since you have not attained the higher concentrations, you are but a commoner.

Thereupon, he drew his sword and severed the Immortal’s hands and feet. Seeing that the Immortal’s countenance remained unmoved, the King then asked, "Do you harbor resentment toward me? The Immortal said:
"I harbor no resentment. I vowed that when I attained Buddhahood, I would deliver the King first. Now that I have realized the Way, I have delivered Cunda first;
he was none other than King Kali.
Śāriputra encountered Aśvajit on the road and, having transmitted his words, attained the vision of the Truth."
In Sanskrit he is called Śāriputra; here it is translated as "Son of the Śāri. He was named after his mother.

Initially, he was a disciple of the non-Buddhist teacher Sañjaya and was profoundly versed in the eighteen great treatises, possessing unrivaled eloquence. Nevertheless, he often lamented that both what he had studied and his teacher were neither true nor correct.
Furthermore, he held the practices and conduct of the non-Buddhists in contempt as being coarse and evil. One day, while traveling on the road...
He encountered the bhikṣu Aśvajit, who was holding his staff and carrying his alms bowl, his robes neatly arranged, and walking with slow and elegant steps.
Delighted, [the seeker] asked him, "Who is your teacher? Aśvajit replied, "The Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, is my teacher. He asked again, "What Dharma does he teach?
He answered, "I have been a renunciant for but a short time and lack a powerful memory; I shall now briefly explain it with one..."
He pointed out the meaning through a verse, saying: "All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they likewise cease from causes and conditions.
My Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, always speaks thus. At that moment, Śāriputra attained realization upon hearing these words. "Truth" (tattva) refers to the ultimate reality.
Aśvajit was Ājñātakauṇḍinya, one of the five bhikṣus first converted at the Deer Park;
Kaundinya followed in his footsteps to serve as a teacher, leading his disciples to return together [to the Dharma].
The one known as Śaṅkhakuśika was the same clan as Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Previously, he had studied under the same teacher as Śāriputra and once made a pact, saying:
"If you obtain the nectar of immortality, I pray that we share it together.
On that day, seeing Śāriputra returning with a serene and joyful countenance, he asked him, "Has my elder brother attained the supreme Dharma? Śāriputra then recounted his encounter. Furthermore—
He demonstrated this through verse, and Maudgalyāyana likewise realized the true principle. They said to one another, "The teachings of the non-Buddhists are merely a waste of effort.
With one mind, the two of them each led their two hundred and fifty disciples to join the Buddha and leave the household life. The Buddha commanded them, "Come, well-come!
and their hair and beards fell away, and the *kāṣāya* robes appeared upon their bodies. The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "These two disciples, Śāri..."
Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers.
Kāśyapa of the Fire-Worshipping Sect (Āgniveśya) subdued his mind by following the tracks of the deer and led his followers to turn their seats [toward the Buddha].
Kāśyapa of the Fire-Worshipping Sect belonged to the clan of Uruvilvā and was an outsider who practiced fire-worship. Because the Buddha wished to transform him, [he acted as he did].

He went there to seek lodging. Kāśyapa declined, saying he had no guest quarters. The Buddha pointed toward the dragon’s hall. Kāśyapa replied, "The nature of dragons is violent and wicked; I fear they may harm you, O Benevolent One.
The Buddha said, "I have no fear," and immediately adjusted his robes and entered to sit within. When night fell, the dragon returned.
Upon seeing the Buddha, he became enraged and set fire to him. The Buddha entered the *ābhāsvara-samādhi* (Fire-Light Samādhi), and the sky was brilliantly illuminated.
The dragon fled, finding no place to hide, until he saw only the Buddha’s alms bowl, which was cool and refreshing; he then leaped into it.
That night, Kāśyapa saw the fire blazing fiercely and said to his disciples, "That śramaṇa must surely be suffering. When dawn arrived, the Buddha was holding the bowl.

He emerged and showed himself to Kāśyapa. Once his mind had somewhat been subdued, he requested the Buddha to remain for a short while so that he might offer him sustenance; however, he was still unwilling to accept the Dharma.

When the Buddha manifested five hundred supernatural transformations, Kāśyapa finally took refuge [in the Triple Gem]. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he simultaneously shaved his head and left the household life.
With all hindrances exhausted and his mind liberated, he became an Arhat. As for all the implements used for fire-sacrifices...
They all cast [the offerings] into the water. Two younger brothers of his lived downstream; one was named Gayā and the other Nadi. They also worshipped fire and dragons.
Seeing the sacrificial vessels floating in the current, they rushed to investigate. Upon seeing that their elder brother had already become a śramaṇa, they asked him the reason.
Their elder brother preached the Dharma for them, and they, along with their two hundred and fifty followers, went forth under the Buddha.
They left the household life and all realized the fruits of the Way. "Hui" (彚) means a class or category; here, it refers to the class of the *Uruvilvā* brothers.

The two elder brothers followed him, which corresponds to what the *I Ching* says regarding "pulling up the thatch-grass, the whole class advancing together. Each, along with his own followers, abandoned fire-worship to serve the Buddha; hence it is said they "turned their seats" (*huixi*).
There is nothing that does not sweetly receive the great downpour of nectar, which universally responds through the *maṇi* jewel.
"Nectar" (*amṛta*) refers to the supreme flavor of the heavens; it is a metaphor for the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.

"Maṇi" (also called *mani*) means "stainless" (*vimala*); it is a precious gem. Because the substance of this jewel is perfectly lustrous, it manifests colors in accordance with whatever object it encounters.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s sovereignty: responding universally to the capacities of all beings and bestowing the Dharma according to their faculties.
Regarding the realms of gods and humans:
as for the realm of gods, twenty-seven days after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he was in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, where the Heavenly King...
He requested that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* be preached. Later, he further preached the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* there.
He preached the *Mañjuśrī-sahasrabhojana-sūtra* in the celestial palace of Maheśvara.

In the Universal Radiance Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he preached the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cittaviśeṣa-sūtra*, and also preached the Dharma for three months during the summer retreat for his mother, Māyā.
...and so forth. Regarding the "human realm," this refers to places such as the five regions of India and the sixteen great kingdoms.
As for the "parrot grove" and the "charnel ground":
regarding the parrot grove, the *Śatavārakajātaka-sūtra* states that the Buddha traveled from Śrāvastī toward the kingdom of Magadha. In the midst [of his journey]...

Along the way, there was a grove of parrots. The king of the parrots, together with his retinue, flew into the palace and invited the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks, saying, "I pray that you will stay one night in my grove so that I may offer you sustenance. The Buddha granted his consent.
Together with the monks, he entered the grove and sat down. When the flock of parrots beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs and his radiant light, as well as the majestic presence of the monks—
Their deportment was serene; each gave rise to joy and faith and passed away on the same day, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding the "charnel ground" (śmaśāna), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: Once the Buddha was staying on the bank of the Ganges River in a forest of corpses.
At that time, the World-Honored One took a few leaves from a tree and addressed the bhikṣus: "Are there more leaves in my hand now, or all those [leaves] upon the great trees?"
"The leaves on the earth are many. The bhikṣus said, "World-Honored One, all the leaves upon the great earth are beyond measure and calculation;

those in the Tathāgata’s hand are too few to mention. The Buddha said, "All the dharmas that I have awakened to are like the grasses, trees, and leaves of the great earth; those that I have proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings are like the leaves in my hand."
Or the Śarabhaṅga Lake:
at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, there was the Śarabhaṅga Lake, where the Buddha preached the sixteenth assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.

Or Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata), located in the city of Rājagṛha; in Sanskrit it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata. It was there that the Buddha preached the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra, and other various sūtras.
Alternatively, in a palace within the ocean,
the Buddha was in the midst of the Great Cloud Maṇi-Treasury Pavilion at the auspicious site of the Nanda Dragon King’s palace,
preaching the *Mahāmegha-parivarta-varṣa-prārthana-sūtra*.
Or Āmrapālīvana;
"āmra" is the name for the *āmalaka* fruit, and this grove was planted with many such fruits. It was there that the Buddha preached the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* and other sūtras.
Or it refers to the Monkey River (*Markaṭahrada*).

Near the city of Vaiśālī was the Monkey Pond (*Markaṭahrada*). Upon the pond stood a mountain hermitage where the Buddha entered the Immovable Samādhi (*āniñjya-samādhi*) and delivered five hundred merchants, all of whom attained the realization of Arhatship.
At that time, the great assembly questioned the Buddha regarding the past causes and conditions of the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā and the five hundred merchants.
Or, it was the Fire Dragon Cave.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that to the west of the city of North India, there is a great cavern where the Nāga King Gopā resides.
When this dragon suddenly conceived an evil intent, wishing to harm the king and destroy the kingdom, the Buddha, knowing this, exercised his supernormal powers and went there.
When the Dragon King saw the Buddha, he was filled with joy, and his evil thoughts ceased. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him and conferred upon him the precept against killing.
Thereupon, the Dragon King requested that the Buddha remain there to accept his offerings. The Buddha said, "I am about to enter parinirvāṇa;
I shall now leave my shadow for you until after my passing. If evil thoughts arise within you, you should contemplate my shadow. He then dispatched five...

One hundred arhats dwell here to receive your offerings and serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Because of this, the kingdom, its cities, and its towns shall forever be free from sorrow and calamity.
The record states that the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty personally went there to pay homage and make offerings.
When viewed from afar, the Buddha’s shadow is brilliantly radiant and golden; yet when approached closely, it cannot be seen.
Or he resided at Vārāṇasī—
properly called Vārāṇasī in the Sanskrit language, and "Country Encircled by Rivers" in the Chinese language— where the Buddha preached such sūtras as the *Udānavarga*,
the *Śālistamba*, and the *Dharmacakrapravartana*.
Sometimes he resided in Magadha—
translated in Chinese as the "Country Without Hatred or Harm"— where the Buddha preached such sutras as the Avataṃsaka, the Nidāna, and the Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish;
or sometimes he stayed at the Venuvana (the Bamboo Grove).
In Sanskrit it is called *śāla*; here it is translated as "Solid. Dharma Master Yao translated it as "Solid Forest.
This refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and other scriptures that the Buddha preached at the very end before his passing.
Sometimes he stayed at the Music Tree in the city of Vaiśālī,

where the Buddha, dwelling beneath the tree, preached the *Anuttara-saṃbodhi-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Sutra on Attaining Liberation through the Consecration that Eradicates Birth and Death). At other times,
he was on the peak of Laṅkā by the seashore.
The mountain is located on the seashore of South India. In Sanskrit it is called Laṅkā; in the language of China it means "Inaccessible.
Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) may reach it. The Buddha resided there and preached a sutra titled the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
Or it may be at Mount Potalaka on a mountain ridge;
in Sanskrit it is called *Potalaka*, which is now corruptedly abbreviated as *Putuo*.
This means "White Flower," referring to the fact that this mountain abounds in such flowers whose fragrance is perceived from afar. It is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Buddha preached the *Ekādaśamukha-avalokiteśvara-sūtra* there.
Alternatively, it was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
"Kalandaka" in Sanskrit means "good sound" (*kalyāṇa-ghoṣa*) in the language of China; it is the name of a bird from the Western Regions, namely the kalandaka.
The elder, a kinsman of King Prasenajit, jointly offered a donation to establish a vihāra and invited the Buddha and his assembly to reside there.
This was either in Śrāvastī— known in the local language as Jintu (金地),
in Sanskrit as Śrāvastī, colloquially called Shewei (舍衛), and in Chinese as "City of Renowned Things" (聞物城)— wherein there dwelt an elder.

His name was Sudatta; in the language of China, it means "Good Giver. He constantly provided relief to the orphaned and the poor, and was highly esteemed by the people of the country, who called him the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver of Alms to the Destitute).
He went to the city of Rājagṛha to seek a wife for his son at the home of the Elder Jīvaka.
He saw that his house was fully prepared with incense, flowers, and food offerings for the following day’s invitation to the Buddha. Sudatta had previously followed non-Buddhist teachers;
upon first hearing the name of the Buddha, his heart grew cold and his hair stood on end. That very night, he went to pay homage to the Buddha and hear the Dharma.

Immediately, his past karma was transformed, and he attained right faith, realizing the first fruit of the path (*srotāpatti*). He then invited the Buddha to return to his kingdom, and the Buddha granted his request. Upon [the Buddha's arrival],...
He returned home and sought out an auspicious site. Only the garden of Prince Jeta was high, airy, and spacious enough to build a vihāra.
He went to inform the prince, who said jokingly, "If you cover the entire garden with gold, then I shall sell it.
Sudatta rejoiced and said, "This garden is now mine. Returning home, he transported gold to spread over eighty *krośas* (or *geng*), and thus purchased it.
He acquired it and established a vihāra called Jetavana. That monasteries are now referred to as "Golden Ground" (Jinti) or "Golden Field" (Jintian) is due to this.
Alternatively, they may appear in emptiness according to one's thoughts.
After King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā had met the Buddha and gained faith in the Dharma, they spoke together:
"Our daughter, Vaidehī Śrīmālā, is wise, of sharp faculties, and quick to understand. If she were to see the Buddha, she would surely attain the Way swiftly.

It would be well to send a messenger to inform her. Upon hearing of the Buddha’s virtues, Śrīmālā received them with joy and reverence, and she praised the Buddha with a verse, saying: "May the Buddha..."
"Out of compassion, you have allowed me to behold you. As she was thinking this, Śākyamuni Tathāgata suddenly manifested an incomparable body in the sky.
Upon seeing him, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha and spoke fifteen chapters, including the "Ten Acceptances" and the "Three Vows."
It is titled the Śrīmālā-sūtra.
Alternatively, [the Buddha] vanished from the mountain and appeared in the palace.
The Buddha vanished from Vulture Peak Mountain and appeared in the Trāyastriṃśa Palace; he vanished from Mount Sumeru and appeared in the Yāma Palace, and so forth.
Having arrived, he spoke as above regarding the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras, or explained that the Dharma is provisionally established according to the six directions.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "The Elder’s Son Śrīgupta addressed the Buddha, saying: 'The various teachers of the non-Buddhists teach...'"
"People worship the six directions in the early morning and thereby obtain long life and wealth. Is there such a worship within the Buddha-dharma? The Buddha said, "There is indeed.
That which is called worshipping the eastern direction is the *dānapāramitā*; worshipping the southern direction is the *śīlapāramitā*;
worshipping the western direction is the *kṣāntipāramitā*; and worshipping the northern direction is the *vīryapāramitā*."
The *pāramitā*s. Pay homage to the *dhyāna-pāramitā* of the lower direction; pay homage to the *prajñā-pāramitā* of the upper direction.
If one can daily perform correct contemplation, prostration, and offerings, one will immediately attain longevity, wealth, and nobility.
Alternatively, he manifested a transformation body three feet tall.

Fearing that the householder Śreṇika was also three feet tall, the Buddha, in order to teach and transform him so that he might return to the True Dharma, likewise manifested a transformation body three feet tall.
As the Sūtra says: "For those who should be delivered by this kind of body, he immediately manifests this body."
This refers to the manifestation of speech through the Dharma.
Or, the palm may be inverted and the fingers transformed.
Regarding the inversion of the palm, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The World-Honored One stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand of Jambūnada gold."
Immediately, the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways. The Tathāgatas dwelling in those worlds, as numerous as motes of dust, each emitted precious light;
simultaneously, they came to the Jeta Grove and poured it over Ānanda’s head. As for the transformation by pointing:
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: The Brahma King Śikhin said to Śāriputra, "I see this land as being like the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Śāriputra replied, "I see this land filled with hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, and replete with filth and impurity."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his toe, and at that very moment,
this trichiliocosm was entirely adorned with the seven treasures, just like the Buddha-land of Ratnavyūha.
Sometimes light flows forth as Buddhas arrive, or a single body manifests universally as many bodies. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
when the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna desired to see the various emanated Buddhas of Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One then emitted light from the mark between his eyebrows, which shone everywhere throughout the ten directions, reaching five hundred million nayutas [of worlds] in each.
From Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of other rivers, at that time each of those Buddhas, taking a single great bodhisattva as an attendant, all came to this land.
All such Buddhas were transformation bodies manifested by Śākyamuni Buddha.
Alternatively, this realm may be clarified by means of other realms.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, when Lady Vaidehī sought rebirth in the Pure Land, the World-Honored One immediately manifested the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
allowing Vaidehī to observe them with her own eyes and choose where she wished to be born.
As for the "place," Vaidehī pointed directly to the land of Amitābha Buddha, saying, "I wish to be born there. The Buddha taught her the cultivation of the sixteen contemplations;
alternatively, one may transform the defiled with the pure, using the pure to cover over the defiled.

In the *Buddha-fangbian-baon jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Skillful Means), the Buddha emits a great light that illuminates the buddha-fields of the ten directions, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas arrive.
At that time, the Sahā world is devoid of mountains, rivers, forests, marshes, and the like.

Furthermore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the earth is transformed three times, becoming adorned and purified throughout the ten directions. Additionally, in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), for the sake of the great assembly, the Buddha...
He manifested inconceivable supernatural transformations, causing a single buddha-field to enter immeasurable buddha-fields, and immeasurable buddha-fields to enter a single buddha-field;
the pure appeared as impure, and the impure appeared as pure.
Either one follows the conventional to clarify the ultimate by means of the conventional;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha does not transcend the two truths. The two truths are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Some say that while remaining within the conventional truth, the principle returns to the reality of the ultimate. Some say that the conventional is itself the ultimate. Or, through the conventional, one clarifies the ultimate. — *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra)
In the Sūtra, King Prasenajit asked: "Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth?
The Buddha said: "I now have nothing to say; you now have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and hearing is called 'one meaning' and 'two meanings.
Furthermore, sixteen kings all had this thought: "The World-Honored One possesses great compassion and brings benefit to all. We, like [others]..."
What is the protection of the state? It is because the Tathāgata, on this account, spoke of the Bodhisattva’s protection of the Buddha-fruit through the truly profound *prajñā*.
It is like an empty valley responding to an echo, or a great bell awaiting a strike.
This is the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma in accordance with the capacities and responses of sentient beings.
Among these, he taught the four *āgamas* and the eightfold emptiness (*aṣṭa-śūnyatā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

The Buddha taught these two teachings within the first thirty years after his attainment of enlightenment; this was because he applied them according to the capacities and dispositions of those present. (From the *Fanwang jing*)

When he had finished speaking and was about to enter nirvana, he said, "Observe this closely: that which exists today shall be gone tomorrow.
Thereupon, he rose from his jeweled couch into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees; having done this seven times, he returned once more to the jeweled couch.
The sun and moon are like falling fireflies; how could they remain for long?
The lifespan of the sun and moon devas is five hundred years, which corresponds to one million eight hundred thousand years in the human realm.
Compared to a human lifespan of one hundred years, it is like a firefly. The *Sūtra Taught to King Prabhāsa* states that the sun and moon possess deities.
Exerting its power, it emits great radiance that illuminates the entire world, yet finally it fades away and disappears. The *Anityatā-sūtra* says:
"The great earth, the sun, and the moon—when their time comes, they all return to extinction."
I admonish you that this body is impermanent so that you may not be heedless.
This body—composed of the four great elements, the five aggregates, and thirty-six constituent factors—is impermanent; yet ordinary people and non-Buddhists reckon it to be permanent.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "In the past, for your sake, throughout immeasurable kalpas..."
Having sacrificed body, life, and wealth to seek unsurpassed bodhi, you should therefore extensively practice after my parinirvāṇa,
quickly emerge from the three realms of existence, and never again be indolent, distracted, or negligent. This is the Tathāgata’s final exhortation.
Thereupon, he returned to ascend the jade throne and lay his head toward the Crane Forest (*Haelin*).
"Returned to ascend" means that the Tathāgata descended from the void. "Jade throne" refers to the precious couch upon which he lay.
"Lay his head" means he lay with his head to the north; for in India, the north is considered the direction of honor, and it also symbolizes the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*.

Later, because the Dharma remained flourishing for a long time in Northern India, there was a tree at the site of the Buddha’s nirvana. In Sanskrit it is called *śāla*; in the vernacular language it means "firm.
There were two trees in each of the four directions, totaling eight. They were five *zhang* high, with branches joined at the top but separated at the base.
When the Buddha passed away, these trees withered and changed color like white cranes; thus, it is called the "Cranes’ Grove" (*Heli*).
The gate of the Samādhi of Universal Roaming is intended to restore the nature of the Single Truth.
"Samādhi" means right concentration; it is that by which all sages proceed, and is therefore called a "gate. The "nature of the Single Truth" is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Great Nirvāṇa is the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas."

"Entering in reverse, entering in forward order, full leaps, and half-leaps"—this describes the gate of the Samādhi of Universal Wandering. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When the Tathāgata was about to enter Parinirvāṇa..."

One enters the first dhyāna; from the first dhyāna one enters and emerges from the second dhyāna, and so on up to the heaven of the fourth formless attainment (ākāśānantyāyatana). One enters the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

This is called "sequential entry" (anuloma-praveśa). If, emerging from the attainment of cessation, one enters the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), and so on down to emerging from the first dhyāna, this is called "reverse entry" (pratiloma-praveśa).
Or, if one enters the third dhyāna from the first dhyāna and emerges from it, or enters the sphere of infinite space from the third dhyāna and emerges from it.

If one enters the first dhyāna and emerges from the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called "full-leaping. Having thus practiced the leaping dhyānas for seven cycles, he then addressed the great assembly:
"With my Buddha-eye, I have universally observed all phenomena within the three realms. The fundamental limit of ignorance is, by its very nature,"
Liberation. By these causes and conditions, I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence, which is named Mahāparinirvāṇa;
it relies upon the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the four *dhyānas* and the perfect stillness of the three dots (*bindu*).

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The World-Honored One, beneath the śāla grove upon his precious couch, entered the fourth dhyāna at the middle watch of the night and remained in profound stillness, then attained parinirvāṇa.

Regarding *samādhi*: in Sanskrit it is called *samādhi*, which means the equal and impartial maintenance of a single collection of mind and mental factors, causing them not to be scattered and allowing them to deeply apprehend the object of focus; this is termed [samādhi].
Samādhi is one of the seven meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Here, it refers to reliance upon the four *dhyānas*, which collectively constitute the fundamental concentrations.

In Sanskrit, they are called *dhyāna*, which is translated here as "meditative contemplation" (*jinglü*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In this concentration, concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium."

Other concentrations that lack these [factors] are not called *dhyāna*. This [term] applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and to states with mind (*sacittaka*), but does not apply to mindless states (*acittaka*).
"Serene" (*zhan*) means tranquil. Regarding the three dots, see the note on the character *ī* above. "Perfect tranquility" (*yuanji*) refers to *nirvāṇa*.
In Sanskrit it is called *parinirvāṇa*; this is translated as "perfect tranquility. "Perfect" (*yuan*) means that there are no virtues that are not complete; "tranquility" (*ji*)...
This means that there are no obstructions left unexhausted; therefore, what is now called *nirvāṇa* is also an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term.

In full, it should be *parinirvāṇa*, which in the language of China means "universal culmination. This refers to the fact that all afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been universally brought to their ultimate end.
At that time, humans and devas cried out and fell prostrate; birds and beasts wailed in grief; whirlwinds blew and clouds gathered suddenly; mountains roared and waves surged backward.

According to the *Lunheng* of ancient and modern times, the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa corresponds to the fifty-second year of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty in this land, the *renshen* year.
It was the fifteenth day of the second month of the year. On this day, a violent wind suddenly arose, destroying people’s houses and snapping down trees.

"A Sage from the West has entered parinirvāṇa; these signs of mourning have appeared. This is as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* by the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda.

He commanded the strongmen to lift it, but in the end none were able to move it.

Terrified and overcome with grief, she fainted. At that moment, the Tathāgata’s golden coffin opened of its own accord. He rose, joined his palms in greeting, and inquired after his compassionate mother, saying:
“You have traveled so far down here; such is the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Pray, do not weep. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, asking:
“If people in the future should ask about this, how should one respond? The Buddha said: “Simply say: ‘After the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa*, Lady Māyā descended [to see him].’”
"Come! For the sake of future unfilial sentient beings, the Buddha has arisen from the golden coffin. Joining his palms in greeting, he should answer thus.
Thereupon, the golden coffin rose of its own accord and circumambulated the great city of Kuśinagara.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: Desiring to cause all sentient beings to attain equal merit, the golden coffin of the Tathāgata rose spontaneously into the air and proceeded slowly.
Devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits followed and circumambulated him, making offerings with incense, flowers, and music.
From the western gate of Kuśinagara City he entered and exited through the eastern gate; from the southern gate he entered and exited through the northern gate. Thus it was.
He entered and exited this way for seven cycles. After the people had finished their veneration and offerings, he then proceeded himself to the top of the incense-altar for cremation;
yet the precious torch would not ignite, halting the grand ceremony of the *jāva* (cremation).
In Sanskrit this is called *jāva*, which here means "cremation. A sutra states: "All humans and devas held precious torches, wishing to ignite the fragrant wood;
yet when the fire reached it, it was extinguished. Ānanda addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata was waiting for Mahākāśyapa, and therefore it has not yet been ignited."
There was none who did not know that Ajātaśatru, while in Rājagṛha, first conceived a dream of the World-Honored One of Ten Epithets, the Compassionate Honored One.
"Ajātaśatru" is the minor name of King Ajātaśatru, the lord of Rājagṛha. At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
The King was lying ill when he had five ominous dreams; upon waking, he learned that the Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa. The ten titles are:
Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara-puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.
"Compassion" (maitrī) is one of the four immeasurable minds (brahmavihāra), specifically great compassion.
Mahākāśyapa descended from afar to Mount Kukkuṭapāda to pay homage to the Buddha’s thousand-spoked wheel-marked feet.
As for Mount Kukkuṭapāda, it has three peaks shaped like the outspread feet of a cock; thus it is named Kukkuṭapāda Mountain.
Mahākāśyapa resided there, far from the city of Kuśinagara. Upon hearing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, he did not employ his supernormal powers [to travel]. Taking...
The assembly of five hundred rushed toward the Twin Sala Trees, arriving only after seven days. The Buddha extended his two feet from outside the coffin to show them to them.
Kāśyapa gazed upon them in worship and wept with grief. Seeing the thousand-spoked wheel marks on the soles of the feet, brilliant and radiant in color like gold, he recited verses of praise.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata uttered a great voice: "I entrust the Eye of the True Dharma to you; you shall..."
Having made it his support, the Buddha’s feet then returned to the coffin as before.
When this was finished, he used fine *tūla* cotton wool to wrap the holy body and cremated himself by means of the sacred fire.
*Tūla* is Indian cotton; *caṇḍa-keśara* is a precious cloth from India.
[The body] was wrapped in its entirety according to the funeral rites of a Cakravartin king. When the fire would not ignite, Kāśyapa said:
"The Tathāgata’s adamantine body cannot be burned by worldly fire. Thereupon, through the power of great compassion, the Tathāgata [emerged] from his heart...
From within the svastika, fire surged forth and ignited itself naturally; therefore, it is called the "sacred fire.
It burned the sandalwood fuel of the royal assembly and poured the water from the golden vase of Śakra.
The fragrant wood for the cremation was all offered by celestial kings and human kings; hence it is called "the sandalwood of the royal assembly.

Śakra first informed the Buddha, requesting that he be granted half of his bodily relics to return to the heavens for veneration. The Buddha consented only to one tooth from the upper palate of his right cheek.
When the fire had already consumed the body, the fierce flames did not subside for seven days. The Dragon King then formed a thought to extinguish them.
They extinguished this fire. First, they took up the relics; though they exerted all their strength, they could not douse it.
Only when Śakra, Lord of Devas, personally held a golden pitcher and poured water upon it did the fire finally subside.

He saw that of the thousand layers of cotton wool wrapped around the Buddha’s body, only those directly touching the body—and the two most superior layers—remained intact in the middle. All the other layers had been reduced to ashes, yet the cranial bone remained as it was.

The tusk remained brilliant and unmoving. Śakra, having received this instruction, took only the single permitted tusk and brought it back to his celestial palace, where he erected a stūpa to enshrine and make offerings to it. This is the fourth stūpa in the heavens.
The power of his vows remains and his compassionate heart still permeates his supreme body of indestructible vajra, which has been reduced to the relic-bones of śarīra.

All Buddhas, from the moment they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, possess four vows. The first is: "Those who have not yet crossed over, may I cause them to cross. And as for sentient beings...

As long as the realms of existence are not exhausted, my vows shall likewise remain unexhausted. Therefore, within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and from within great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), I manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to extensively deliver sentient beings.
Although I manifest parinirvāṇa, I leave behind relics (*śarīra*) to circulate throughout the world.

To cause others to offer reverence and support, thereby generating the aspiration for goodness, it is said that "the power of his vows still remains" and "his compassionate heart continues to permeate.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "By means of the supreme Vajra-samādhi, he shattered his own vajra-body, yet without abandoning great compassion, his relics were still distributed."
Thereupon, the eight kingdoms arrayed their fourfold armies with solemn dignity, each holding its own golden casket and vying to return it to the precious stūpa.
As for the eight kingdoms:
they were the powerful nations of India. As for the fourfold armies: they consisted of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. As for the *dīrgha* (casket): it is a jar.
It was made of gold. In Sanskrit it is called *sūrpaka*, which here means "jeweled stūpa.
Generally, any structure made of wood, earth, brick, or stone that contains the relics (*śarīra*) of the Buddha is termed a jeweled stūpa. The *Bodhisattva Garbha Sūtra* states:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were eight *hu* and four *dou* of relics. Eight kings, each arraying their fourfold army, came to contend for them. Thereupon—
When the eight classes of gods and dragons all rose up with vying hearts, a wise minister said: "If the kings contend, there must be victory and defeat;
thus the Tathāgata’s relics will not bring about benefit. I shall divide them into three portions:

one portion I will offer to the devas, one portion I will give to the nāgas and spirits, and one portion I will distribute among the eight kingdoms. By this means, the hearts of the multitude were gladdened.
Each took [a portion] and stored it in a golden jar, then escorted them back to their own countries to erect stupas for veneration.
Thus, whether it was the tooth or the hair, Kāśyapa paid homage to them in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace.
The Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, established four stūpas:

The meaning of the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (akṣaya-pradīpa) found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* lies herein. When the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, he entrusted [the Dharma] to Mahākāśyapa;
Kāśyapa, upon his own nirvana, entrusted it to Ānanda; and Ānanda, upon his own nirvana, entrusted it to Śāṇavāsa.
From that point downward, through twenty-seven patriarchs, the lineage was transmitted one-to-one. Thus, Guifeng said: "The former patriarchs were in the era of chaotic beginnings."
To prevent loss, it was transmitted from one person to another; thus, through successive generations, there has been a basis for reliance.
Wherever a thousand lamps shine, there is none that does not see Mahākāśyapa welcomed by a multitude of thousands amidst clouds.
