Upāli dispatched a messenger to the summit of Mount Meru to strike a bronze *ghanṭā*. From the sound of the bell, a voice proclaimed:
"Summon all the noble disciples who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), numbering one thousand, to the Piṇḍava Cave at Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha.
King Ajātaśatru has been invited to serve as the patron (*dānapati*) and external protector for the compilation of the Master’s bequeathed teachings."
Ānanda-lekhu-saṃcakra. In Sanskrit, Ānanda;
in the language of China, Qìngxǐ (Joyful Celebration). He was the Buddha’s cousin on his mother’s side. After renouncing the household life, he served as the Buddha’s attendant for twenty years.
He was foremost among those of great learning (*bahuśruta*). During the initial *saṃgīti* (council), only those who were *aśaikṣa* (non-learners) and noble ones (*ārya*) were admitted.
At that time, Ānanda was still at the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*). Having been dismissed from the assembly by Kāśyapa, Ānanda felt frustrated and resentment;
he then practiced the meditative concentrations of the higher stages in the forest, severed the remaining bonds of afflictions, and immediately realized the fruit of arhatship.

He immediately came to the gate and addressed the assembly, requesting entry. Kāśyapa said to him, "If you have already attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), you should enter through the crack of the door.
Ānanda entered at these words and paid homage to the great assembly.
Kāśyapa then requested Upāli to compile the Vinaya Piṭaka, while Ānanda compiled the Sūtra Piṭaka. As Ānanda ascended the seat, the assembly had three doubts; the first was as follows:
The Buddha appeared once more. Second, some doubted that a Buddha from another world-system had come; third, others doubted that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood.
When Ānanda proclaimed, "Thus have I heard," all these doubts were dispelled. Regarding the phrase "thundering like a roar," the *Dharmapada-sūtra* states:
"The bhikṣu Mahālu-dakṣiṇa’s voice was like the roar of thunder. Some compare Ānanda to him. The "three wheels" refers to the sound.
The tongue is speech. Yet sound possesses five virtues: first, it is as profound as thunder; second, it is clear and heard from afar; third, listeners never tire of it;
fourth, it enters the heart and is cherished; fifth, it is precise and easy to understand. Ānanda possessed these qualities;
therefore, it is said that his voice roared like thunder throughout the three spheres.
Śāṇavāsa manifested his supernormal power regarding the future.
While the Tathāgata was traveling through the country of Mathurā, he pointed to a grove of blue trees and said to Ānanda:
"This is called Mount Uruvilvā. After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall establish [the Dharma] here."
In the monastery, he preached the Dharma and transformed beings, bringing great benefit to many. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a disciple of Ānanda named Śāṇakavāsin.
As Ānanda was about to pass away, he entrusted the Dharma to him. He extensively practiced the work of transformation, exactly as the Buddha had foretold.
Śāṇakavāsin took the elder Upagupta as his disciple. One day, [Śāṇakavāsin] went to his location.
As he sat upon the couch, all of Kātyāyanīputra’s disciples failed to recognize him and mostly gave rise to arrogant thoughts.
Śāṇakavāsin then raised his hand into the air, whereupon a rain of nectar fell and five hundred Dharma-gates were manifested. Kātyāyanīputra did not recognize them, so Śāṇakavāsin said:
When the Buddha entered this meditative absorption, Maudgalyāyana did not comprehend it; when Maudgalyāyana entered [absorption], the bhikṣus did not comprehend it;
when I enter [absorption], you do not recognize it. I have attained seventy-seven thousand Jātaka-sūtras, eighty thousand Vinaya texts, and eighty thousand Abhidharma texts.
"You all do not understand. If I depart, the various Dharma-gates will follow me.
Guptaka transformed counting-sticks (*śalākā*) until they filled the room.
Upagupta was a disciple to whom the Dharma was entrusted by Śāṇakavāsin. During the time when the Buddha was still in the world, there was a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).
The Nirgrantha named Satyaka was intelligent, eloquent, and proficient in various treatises; all the kings honored him as their teacher.
However, knowing that the Buddha’s Dharma was correct and sublime, he desired to leave the household life and came to address the Buddha, saying:
"If I were to leave the household life, would I be able to become like the Buddha? The Buddha said: "No. He asked again: "Would I be like Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, or even..."
The question was asked: "Is it as you have said? The Buddha replied to all that they were not yet so. He continued:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are no great beings [to maintain the Dharma], only then will it be so. The Buddha said to the assembly:

"When about one hundred years have passed since my parinirvāṇa, a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) will be born in the kingdom of Mathurā, named Upagupta—'Upagupta' meaning 'Near Protector' in the language of China. He will leave the household life, realize the fruits of the path, and perform conversions."
The number of people was beyond counting. When the appointed time arrived, everything occurred exactly as the Buddha had prophesied.

While preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings in Central India, whenever a lay couple who had received his instruction attained the Way together, they would cast a tally-stick (*śalākā*) into a stone chamber.

The chamber was two *zhang* high and three *zhang* in both length and width; eventually, the tally-sticks completely filled it. This continued until the parinirvāṇa of Kātyāyanīputra, whose disciple was named... [text ends].
Regarding the *tongzhenliang* (measures for penetrating the truth): one uses only these tally-sticks (*chou*) for the cremation (*jiewei*).

Beginning with the omen of the collapsing beam, when Mahākāśyapa was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, after he had entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda, he took up the robe bestowed by the Buddha and entered the *kī*...

He then went to take his leave, but the king was asleep and did not see him. During the king's sleep, the great beam of the palace hall broke, whereupon he awoke.

"If King Ajātaśatru comes, and when Maitreya descends to be born, only then shall this mountain open. When the king arrived, the mountain opened for him;
he saw Kāśyapa sitting upright within, holding his robes. The king gazed upon him with reverence and wept with grief. After he finished offering verses of praise, the mountain closed once more.
This concludes the account of the omen of the flowing milk.
The twenty-fourth patriarch of the Dharma transmission from the Western Heaven, Venerable Siṃha, was in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
Knowing that a calamity was imminent and could not be evaded, he bestowed a robe and a verse upon his disciple, Venerable Vasudhara.
He said, "I have encountered a great difficulty here; you should go to another country to propagate the teaching.

Subsequently, the non-Buddhists flourished and slandered King Mīlinda, causing the king to lose his correct faith. He then destroyed the Dharma and demolished the monasteries, seizing a sword to strike off the head of the Lion [Śāriputra];
yet white milk gushed forth several feet high. Thus, the transmission of the Dharma in that country ultimately ended with him.
People are like vessels; though the containers differ, the water within is necessarily the same.
The *Āgama* Sūtras state: "Ānanda’s transmission and upholding of the Buddha-dharma is like pouring water from one vessel into another. Vessel and container...
Though the lamps differ, the water remains undivided;
though the lamps are lit separately, the light is ultimately one.

Therefore, within the Great Vehicle’s true emptiness and wondrous existence, Mañjuśrī and Maitreya differ in their respective schools.

The capacities [of sentient beings] vary according to their faculties, and thus there is no lack of distinction between them.

For instance, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva propagated the school of the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*), which establishes as a fact that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Maitreya Bodhisattva propagated the school of the five natures (*pañcaprakṛti*):
first, the śrāvaka nature; second, the pratyekabuddha nature; third, the Mahāyāna nature; and fourth, the indeterminate nature. This indeterminate...
"Nature" (*gotra*) refers to the fact that the eighth consciousness contains the seeds of the three vehicles; when it encounters conditions, these are cultivated.
Therefore, it is called "indeterminate. The fifth is the nature of lacking seeds. This means that within the eighth consciousness there are no seeds of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*);

He roots them and brings them to maturity.

Later, as teachers and disciples transmitted [the teachings] to one another, they fell into mutual contradictions, and the lineages consequently diverged. The *Chusanzang jiji* (Collection of Records Concerning the Translation of the Tripitaka) states:
During the Buddha’s lifetime, there was an elder who dreamed that a precious rug suddenly split into five sections. Terrified, he questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said, "This signifies that after my parinirvāṇa, the Vinaya Piṭaka will be divided into five schools.
Furthermore, according to the *Nidāna Sūtra*, King Bimbisāra dreamed of a single-stick golden staff being broken into eighteen pieces, and he reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "This indicates that after my parinirvāṇa, the teachings of the Hīnayāna will be divided into eighteen schools.

The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was the secular younger brother of the Bodhisattva Asaṅga and his junior disciple in the Dharma; he was the founder of this school.

The Sarvāstivādins composed five hundred treatises to clarify their own school and refute the Mahāyāna; there was no one in India who dared to oppose them. Asaṅga was a Bodhisattva of the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
Observing that his younger brother’s roots and conditions for the Mahāyāna were about to ripen, he feigned illness and summoned him back.

When they were still a single *yojana* (or station) away, he dispatched a disciple to receive him. Upon arriving at night, they stayed together in the same lodging. During the night, that disciple recited [the scriptures].

He repented his past slanders, lamenting that it was too late for such deep remorse to be of any avail. Realizing that the root of his transgression lay solely in his faculty of speech, he then raised his hand [to sever it].
Holding a sharp sword, he intended to cut off [the monk’s] tongue. Asanga perceived this from afar; extending his arm, he seized him and restrained him, admonishing him, saying:
"The time has come for you to realize the Mahāyāna. Since you previously used your tongue to disparage it, you ought now to use that same tongue to praise it, so as to remedy your transgression."
"If one were to simply cut out one's tongue and remain silent, what benefit would there be? Vasubandhu accepted this instruction and desisted.

He traveled by night under the stars until he could visit his original teacher. There, he listened attentively to the compassionate instructions and subsequently composed five hundred Mahāyāna treatises;

Bodhisattva Deva was a disciple of Nāgārjuna; he was brilliant and adept at discerning the meaning of the Dharma, renowned throughout the Five Indias, and resided in South India.
After he initially attained the Dharma, people had not yet placed their faith in him. In that country, there was a temple of Maheśvara where [an image] was cast.

Deva said, "The deity is indeed divine, but why is it so small? It ought to manifest its spiritual power."
This man’s wisdom and virtue had subdued all things, yet he falsely claimed to possess abundant gold; his crystal eyes were merely deceptive illusions, not what one would truly hope for.

Deva then climbed a ladder and gouged out those eyes, whereupon the deity’s spiritual power was instantly extinguished. From this point on, Deva’s reputation and transformative influence spread far and wide.

The deity said, "I shall transform you into a single object; nothing is more long-lived than stone. He then announced to his disciples: "I am about to undergo transformation."
Stone. If anyone were to challenge my treatise, I would have them write it upon this stone, and I myself would provide the response.

In a short while, the text of their reply appeared from within the stone. Dignāga then established another formal inference as his response, and after one night had passed—

Just as he was about to emerge, he reached the fourth syllogism and challenged him with a difficult objection. Śrīlāta was unable to answer. Suddenly, [Dharmakīrti] let out a great roar, which caused the stone to shatter and fly apart with a violent shock.
Thus, it is said in India that Dharmakīrti possessed the power to "roar at the stone."

in the language of China, this means "the Ugly Ones. They are spirits.

"First: The Sangha that saves all is supreme. If there is any scholar from the eight directions capable of refuting this doctrine, I shall cut off his head to atone for my defeat.

"Your hair is no different from that of the dead. Thereupon, the scholars of the eight directions all shaved their heads and left the household life.
They used elephants adorned with the precepts to carry gold and invited Vasubandhu.

Consequently, Vasubandhu himself composed a prose commentary on the verses; this is the present *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

He died without regret. Vasubandhu read his treatise and saw that its arguments largely accorded with his own views;

A thousand years later, the teachings and their resonance will arrive here. What Your Majesty dreamed of is precisely this event.

At that time, Emperor Ming accepted the petition of Wang Zun and dispatched eighteen men, including the General of the Household Cai Xin, the Grand Master Tai Jing, and the Doctor Wang Zun, to travel together to the Western Regions to invite the Buddha-dharma.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Yuezhi, they encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan.
Two Indian monks arrived together with a white silk painting of Śākyamuni and the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*.

Emperor Ming issued an edict to have images of Śākyamuni painted upon the West Yang Gate and at the Xianjie Mausoleum.
This was the beginning of the practice of making offerings to images in this land. The eminent Tang monk and Great Vinaya Master Daoxuan resided at Mount Zhongnan.
Because his moral integrity and observance of the precepts were supreme, the Vaiśravaṇa King of Northern India constantly dispatched two celestial beings to protect him in secret.
Once, while Daoxuan was walking in meditation, he lost his footing and was about to fall down the steps; at that moment, a celestial being...
When people stepped upon his feet, he would manifest his body. They asked him why he was called a "Heavenly Man" (deva). He replied:
"They are like Su You and Hu Duo of the Zhou dynasty, Fu Yi and Wang Zun of the Han dynasty, and Kan Ze of the Wu dynasty;

all were men who had never previously encountered the Buddha-dharma, yet they were able to know that the teachings of the Sage’s birth and extinction would come in the future and could discern that the Buddha-dharma is supreme. Regarding them...
"Who are they? The celestial being Huang Qiong replied, "They are all celestial beings.
It is because the Buddha-dharma is to circulate in this land that the heavens have sent them to descend as spirits to assist the state and proclaim and clarify the Buddha-dharma."

I, Bo Dao, was born in a degenerate age and have had the fortune to receive the true discourse; yet, though I have recorded and continued [the teachings], I have narrated the golden words while adrift and have not encountered the Jade Sage.

The clarity exceeds that of a mirror opening its case; the mountains and seas are like the high and deep. "Clouds and Thunder" refers to the swift eloquence; the *Mahāvaipulya-śāstra* states:
When the Tathāgata ascends to the realm of emptiness of *nirvāṇa* with remainder, he raises the clouds of great compassion and flashes the lightning of supreme wisdom.
He thunders the sound of emptiness and non-self—this refers to the unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) among the four types of eloquence. It is swift.

This refers to "swift eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) among the seven types of eloquence. Because the Tathāgata possesses these various forms of eloquence, he knows the names, characteristics, phrases, and meanings of all phenomena;
thus, he delights in speaking with ease and fluency, without omission or loss, and because he discerns them with perfect clarity, he is free from fear.

The myriad classes of beings find satisfaction within their own roots.

Regarding the four questions:

It manifests through supernatural transformations and cannot be destroyed by any object. It remains constant throughout immeasurable kalpas, fully endowed with the power of transport.
